title: A lamp to my feet (Psalm 118 [119]:105)
hookLine: thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths
carry: enough light for the next step

cards: You get up in the night for a glass of water. The house is dark. You don't turn on every light.
You tap your phone's flashlight and point it at the floor. It shows about three steps: the edge of the rug, the corner of the table, the doorway. And it's enough.
You don't need to see the kitchen from the bedroom, only the next step, and then the one after that. Long before flashlights, a psalmist had the same thought.

teach.h: A SMALL CLAY LAMP, NOT A FLOODLIGHT.
teach.b: The verse sits in the middle of yesterday's alphabet psalm, at the start of the stanza for the letter nun. In the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." First, picture the lamp.

Not a streetlight or a lighthouse. In ancient Israel a lamp was a small clay dish with olive oil and a wick; the Hebrew word is ner. Hold one up at night and it lights a small circle around your feet.
That's the point: the psalmist isn't promising a floodlight over the whole road. God's word lights the next step. Second, what it doesn't promise.

teach.h: NO MAP, NO VIEW OF NEXT YEAR.
teach.b: It doesn't say you'll see the map, or know where the road bends next year. It's tempting to want the whole route before starting out. The psalm offers something smaller and steadier: enough light to walk by.
Third, why that can be a comfort and not a letdown.
A small light has to be carried close. In the psalm, the walker keeps near the word, one step at a time.
Catholics hear God's word here in two senses: the scriptures they read, and the Word made flesh, Christ, whom Saint John calls the light.

teach.h: THY WORD IS A LAMP TO MY FEET.
teach.b: Jews hear it as the Torah, the teaching that guides daily life. Both read the same verse and hear the same promise: not everything, just enough.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 118 [119], this verse included, in the Liturgy of the Hours, and some say verse 105 before reading scripture.

games.q: you're walking an unfamiliar road at night with a small clay lamp. what does it let you see?
o: the whole road to the end.
the next few steps around your feet.
games.why: just the next few steps. the psalm's promise is small and steady: "a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths."

practice: Think of the next thing you'll walk into today: a room, a meeting, a hard conversation, a school gate. Don't plan the whole day; just see the doorway.
If you pray, say the verse slowly, thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths; if you don't, ask yourself what the next right step is, only the next one.
